name: Interpupillary distance optimisation

card.summary: Interpupillary distance (IPD) is the spacing between the pupils, a measurement looksmaxxers use when judging eye-area balance and when weighing glasses, brow and eye-area changes that alter how the eyes appear to sit.
card.note: Pupil spacing is set by the skull and cannot be changed by non-surgical means; craniofacial surgery for extreme spacing is a medical procedure with real risks.

quick.overview:
Interpupillary distance is the distance in millimetres between the centres of the two pupils. Looksmaxxers treat it, along with related measures such as the inner-corner distance and ratios to facial width, as part of how balanced the eye area looks. The goal of 'optimising' it is usually to understand where one's own spacing sits and to choose styling and eyewear that suit it.

Measurement data are well documented in optometry: a 2012 US Army survey reports a male mean of 64.0 mm and a female mean of 61.7 mm, and studies report differences by age, sex and ethnicity. Bone structure sets the spacing, so changes are done through perception, such as brow shaping, glasses and hairstyle, rather than altering the pupils themselves.
quick.how: People measure with a ruler, a pupillometer or a phone app, often to order glasses, then compare their figure and ratios with population values or with ratios they see discussed online. Some discussions pair it with the brow-ridge-to-IPD ratio, and mention supraorbital implants, brow work or botulinum toxin as ways forum members describe adjusting the eye area's look.
quick.risks: Measuring carries no risk. Very wide or very narrow spacing can occasionally be associated with medical conditions, and optometry literature notes that extreme IPD may predispose to horizontal strabismus. Surgical correction of hypertelorism is major craniofacial surgery with risks including bleeding, infection and cerebrospinal fluid leak.

lead: Interpupillary distance (IPD), also called pupillary distance, is the distance in millimetres between the centres of the pupils. Binocular PD runs pupil to pupil; monocular PD is measured from each pupil to the centre of the nose bridge. It is used mainly to centre prescription lenses and to fit virtual-reality headsets and other binocular devices.[1]

In looksmaxxing communities, IPD is one of the proportions discussed when assessing the eye area. Members compare their eye spacing with typical values and with other measurements such as the browridge-to-IPD ratio, which one looksmax.org thread proposes as a way to quantify how low-set the brow ridge appears.[2] 'Optimising' it in this sense means evaluating where one's spacing sits and choosing styling, eyewear, brow treatments or procedures that change how the eyes read, since the pupils' spacing itself follows the skull.

Optometric and anthropometric research has measured IPD across populations. Values vary with age, sex and ethnicity, and a 2026 systematic review of 243 studies reported that IPD differs between ethnic groups and that extreme values may be associated with horizontal strabismus patterns.[3][1]

angle.text: People use IPD as a reference measurement for the eye area. Because the spacing is skeletal, improvements are described through things that change perception, such as brow grooming, hairstyle, glasses that sit at the right position, or in forum discussions brow-area procedures.

paras: IPD is measured traditionally with a small ruler known as a PD stick, with a corneal-reflex pupillometer placed on the nose bridge, or increasingly with phone and web apps that use a reference object such as a credit card.[1] Eye-care professionals normally measure it at an eye exam.[1]

A 2012 US Army survey reported a mean of 64.0 mm for men (range 53.0 to 77.0) and 61.7 mm for women (range 51.0 to 74.5).[1] Measures that appear in looksmaxxing talk alongside it include the inner canthal distance and the outer orbital distance.

Normative studies show that IPD grows through childhood and that it varies with ethnicity. A study of adults in Hong Kong found IPD similar to values reported for Caucasian groups but larger interorbital and inner canthal distances.[4] An analysis of 1,311 subjects from 1 month to 19 years provided age-based norms for IPD and pupil diameter.[5]

Abnormally wide eye spacing is called hypertelorism and may accompany many congenital conditions. Craniofacial surgery, usually carried out between ages 5 and 8, can reposition the orbits toward the midline; complications can include bleeding, infection, cerebrospinal fluid leaks and double vision.[6]

A looksmax.org thread about browridge-to-IPD ratio gives example values of 6.1 for a male model and 3.30 for the poster and describes a low-set brow ridge as a male-dimorphic feature. The poster lists a supraorbital implant, an upper-eyelid fat graft, a fat graft along the brow ridge or forehead botulinum toxin as options for changing how the eye area looks, noting that botulinum toxin does not change bone.[2] Other replies in the thread debate how the ratio should be read.[2]

No studies found on 'optimising' IPD for appearance. Population-measurement research exists, including the 2026 systematic review of IPD by ethnicity and strabismus patterns,[3] the Hong Kong normative study[4] and the paediatric reference values.[5]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, IPD appears mostly as one input into eye-area ratios rather than as something to change directly.[2]

claims.claim: A low browridge-to-IPD ratio marks a masculine, low-set brow.
claims.believers: The thread's author says men usually have square orbits with a low-set supraorbital bone and uses the ratio to quantify it.[2]
claims.experts: No published study has validated this ratio as a measure of attractiveness; anthropometric research reports IPD and orbital distances themselves.[4][3]
